subject: Archaeology
title: Citizen Science in Archaeology
description: A micro-lesson that makes Citizen Science in Archaeology usable.

hook.text: You do not need a degree. Thousands of volunteers find new archaeological sites from home.

buildup.text: GlobalXplorer lets anyone scan satellite tiles for looting. Over 100,000 have joined.

discovery.text: MicroPasts invites volunteers to 3D-model objects and transcribe old dig records.

twist.text: A volunteer on GlobalXplorer spotted an unrecorded site in Peru that experts missed.

climax.text: Open data makes archaeology democratic. The public is now part of the research team.

punchline.text: You can discover an ancient site from your couch.

quiz.question: What is GlobalXplorer?
options: A GPS app guiding tourists to archaeological sites
A platform where volunteers scan satellite images for looting
A database of every excavated site on Earth

details.summary: Citizen science projects invite non-professionals to contribute to archaeological research through activities like identifying features in satellite imagery, transcribing historical records, and surveying fields for surface finds.
details.whyItMatters: Professional archaeologists cannot survey the entire landscape or process all available data alone. Citizen science multiplies research capacity while engaging the public in heritage preservation and scientific discovery.
takeaways: Volunteers identify archaeological features in satellite images
Public participation dramatically expands research capacity
Projects like GlobalXplorer engage thousands of contributors

faq.question: What is GlobalXplorer and how does it work?
faq.answer: Created by Sarah Parcak, GlobalXplorer asks volunteers to examine satellite imagery tiles and flag potential archaeological features like wall foundations or looting pits. Thousands of participants have surveyed areas across Peru and India, identifying sites that professionals then investigate.

faq.question: How reliable are citizen science contributions to archaeology?
faq.answer: Individual observations are verified through redundancy — multiple volunteers examine the same data, and only consensus identifications are flagged. Professional archaeologists then verify promising identifications. This filtering process produces surprisingly reliable results.
